llm_response.content:
COMPLETE EMPIRICAL RESEARCH PLAN  

──────────────────────────────────────────────  

1. Identification Strategy  
Method: Two-stage least squares (2SLS) IV, where the compulsory-schooling reform is the instrument for parental years of education.  

Why IV?  
• The research question is the causal effect of parental schooling on child schooling. Schooling is choice-driven and correlated with unobserved family ability, so OLS is biased.  
• Norway’s staggered 1959 reform generated large, plausibly exogenous shifts in the lower tail of the parental schooling distribution, varying by birth cohort and municipality.  
• Staggered rollout permits a difference-in-differences first stage (municipality × cohort). The IV combines DiD for relevance with the exclusion restriction needed for causal spillovers.  
• Event-study graphs will diagnose pre-trends; we can also report “reduced-form” (reform → child outcomes) as a robustness check.  

2. Treatment and Control  

Treatment variable (endogenous regressor):  
Parental years of completed schooling (continuous).  For interpretation we will scale by one year.

Instrument (Z):  
ReformExposure_im  = 1 if parent i grew up in municipality m where the 9-year reform had been implemented no later than the calendar year in which that parent turned age 14 (end of compulsory schooling), 0 otherwise.  Formally  

ReformExposure_im = 1[ ReformYear_m  ≤  BirthYear_i  + 7 ]  

Control group:  
Parents from the same birth cohorts (1947–1958) who lived in municipalities that had not yet implemented the reform by the time they turned 14.  

Treatment timing:  
Varies by municipality between 1960 and 1972.  The “event date” is the municipality-specific first September with the new 9-year curriculum in place.

Child outcome Y:  
Years of completed schooling (or indicators for upper-secondary, tertiary, etc.) for children aged 25–35 in 2000.

Main estimating equations  

First stage:  
ParEdu_imc = π ReformExposure_im  + γ_m  + δ_c  + X′_im β  + ε_im  

Second stage:  
ChildEdu_ijc = β1 Ê[ParEdu_imc]  + γ_m  + δ_c  + X′_im β2 + X′_child θ  + u_ij  

• γ_m: municipality-of-parent-childhood fixed effects  
• δ_c: parent birth-cohort fixed effects  
• Standard errors clustered at municipality × cohort (instrument varies at that level).  

3. Key Identifying Assumptions  

A1. Relevance ‑ the reform raised parents’ completed schooling.  
Plausible: prior studies find ≈0.6 additional years at the mean and >80 % drop in “<9 years”.

A2. Independence / quasi-random timing ‑ conditional on γ_m and δ_c, ReformExposure is as-good-as-random.  
Plausible: Parliamentary committee targeted representativeness; Ness (1971) shows no strong predictors.

A3. Exclusion Restriction ‑ the only channel from ReformExposure to child education is through parental education.  
Plausible but must discuss: children are born 1965-1975 and live in 1980-1990 education system, usually outside the parent’s childhood municipality.  Direct exposure is limited, but better-educated parents may move or earn more—those are endogenous and part of the causal chain (allowed).  We must rule out municipality-level shocks that persist into the 1980s; municipality × cohort FE plus controls for 1960 characteristics help.

A4. Monotonicity/SUTVA ‑ nobody’s schooling falls because of the reform; one parent’s treatment does not directly change another parent’s treatment within the same instrument cell.  Highly plausible.

A5. Stable composition ‑ reform does not differentially change survival to age 25 or linkage to children registers in a way correlated with child outcomes.  Plausible in rich Norwegian registers; we can test for migration/attrition.

4. Threats to Identification & Mitigations  

T1. Direct effects on children (school quality spillovers).  
– Use childhood municipality of the parent, not of the child, minimising overlap.  
– Drop children born and schooled in the same municipality as the parent grew up; reproduce results.  
– Include controls for child’s own exposure to post-1970 school spending.

T2. Selective migration of parents after reform-induced education gains.  
– Control for parents’ municipality at age 16 and municipality at child’s birth; interact with reform.  
– Re-estimate on subsample of “stayers” who live in municipality of childhood in 1970 Census.

T3. Fertility selection (reform changes likelihood or timing of having children).  
– Show reduced-form impact of reform on probability of ever having children and age at first birth.  
– Re-weight by inverse propensity of fertility (“Lee bounds” if sizable).  
– Estimate spillovers separately for first-borns where timing issues are smaller.

5. R Code Outline  

```r
# 0. Packages ---------------------------------------------------------------
library(data.table)
library(fixest)
library(ggplot2)
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

# 1. Data loading -----------------------------------------------------------
parents   <- fread("norway_parents.csv")      # one row per parent
children  <- fread("norway_children.csv")     # one row per child
muni_rev  <- fread("municipality_reform.csv") # ReformYear_m column

# 2. Merge and variable construction ---------------------------------------
# Parent-level data with instrument
parents <- merge(parents, muni_rev, by = "municipality_id", all.x = TRUE)
parents[ , reform_exposure := as.integer(ReformYear_m <= birth_year + 7)]

# Collapse child outcomes to parent level (mean years of schooling of kids)
child_avg <- children[, .(child_edu = mean(years_schooling, na.rm = TRUE)), 
                      by = .(parent_id)]
parents   <- merge(parents, child_avg, by = "parent_id", all.x = TRUE)

# Fixed effects identifiers
parents[ , fe_muni  := factor(municipality_id) ]
parents[ , fe_cohort:= factor(birth_year)      ]

# Control variables
parents[ , X := .(sex_parent, age_parent_2000,   # example controls
                  log(real_earnings_1995), 
                  num_siblings_parent) ]

# 3. Main 2SLS specification -----------------------------------------------
iv_formula <- child_edu ~ 1 | 
              reform_exposure ~ years_schooling_parent + 
              fe_muni + fe_cohort + sex_parent + age_parent_2000

mod_2sls <- feols(iv_formula, data = parents, 
                  cluster = ~ municipality_id + birth_year)
summary(mod_2sls)

# 4. Robustness: drop children living in parent’s childhood municipality ----
parents_nodirect <- parents[ child_muni_id != municipality_id ]
mod_rb <- feols(iv_formula, data = parents_nodirect, 
                cluster = ~ municipality_id + birth_year)
summary(mod_rb)

# 5. Event-study for pre-trends (first stage) ------------------------------
# Create event time k = birth_year - ReformYear_m
parents[ , event_time := birth_year - ReformYear_m ]
evt_data <- parents[ abs(event_time) <= 6 ]  # 6-year window

mod_evt  <- feols(years_schooling_parent ~ i(event_time, ref = -1) + 
                  fe_muni + fe_cohort, data = evt_data, 
                  cluster = ~ municipality_id)
iplot(mod_evt)  # ggplot of coefficients
```

6. Expected Results  

Economic theory and prior elasticities suggest a positive intergenerational return.  International estimates range 0.15–0.25 extra child years per additional parental year.  Given Norway’s generous welfare state (diminishing credit constraints) but strong emphasis on early tracking, I expect:  

β1 ≈ 0.20 (i.e., one extra parental year raises child schooling by one-fifth of a year)  
plus ≈ 3–4 p.p. higher probability of completing upper-secondary school.

7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (IV)  

C1: Instrument relevance (F-stat > 10)……………………………………1  
C2: Independence of instrument (no confounders)………………0.8  
C3: Exclusion restriction (no direct child effect)…………………0.7  
C4: Monotonicity / no defiers………………………………………1  
C5: SUTVA / no general-equilibrium spillovers…………………0.8  
Overall score ≈ 4.3 / 5 → credible but must probe C2–C3 with robustness.
